concepts.label: Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Mixtures
concepts.cardText: A mixture of sugar and water has a uniform composition throughout, and a well-stirred mixture is equally sweet in the first and the last sip. Such a mixture is called a homogeneous mixture, or a solution. Other examples are vinegar (acetic acid in water) and aerated drinks like soda (carbon dioxide in water), and a solution always remains homogeneous. A stirred mixture of sand and water is not uniform: the sand particles are easily visible in the water and settle with time. Such a mixture is called a heterogeneous mixture.

concepts.label: Solutions: Solute, Solvent and Concentration
concepts.cardText: Solutions are prepared when a solute, the substance that gets dissolved, is mixed with a solvent, the substance that dissolves the solute. In the mixture of sugar and water, sugar is the solute and water is the solvent. The right proportion is always essential when preparing a solution: Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) needs specified amounts of salt and sugar added to a fixed amount of water, and not all sugary drinks prepared at home or sold in the market are ORS. When farmers spray pesticides they must mix the right amount of pesticide with a fixed amount of water, as too little may not protect crops while too much can damage crops, soil and the environment. The amount of solute dissolved in a given amount of solvent or solution is termed the concentration of the solution.

concepts.label: Expressing Concentration as a Percentage
concepts.cardText: Concentration can be expressed in several ways, a common one being the percentage. Mass by mass percentage (% m/m) tells how many grams of solute are present in 100 grams of the total solution; it is commonly used for homogeneous mixtures, and for heterogeneous mixtures like milk powder and spice mixtures and for labelling packaged foods. Mass by volume percentage (% m/v) is used where measuring the volume of a liquid is easier than weighing it, as in medicines and laboratories, and tells how many grams of solute are present in 100 millilitres of solution, as in a 5% glucose solution. Volume by volume percentage (% v/v) is used when two miscible liquids are mixed, as in perfumes, cosmetics and vinegar, and tells how many millilitres of solute are present in 100 millilitres of solution. A hospital saline drip is usually 0.9 % m/v sodium chloride in water, that is 0.9 g of salt in 100 mL of solution, which is safe for blood and replaces lost fluids in the body.

concepts.label: Solubility, Saturated Solutions and Solubility Curves
concepts.cardText: The maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a fixed quantity of the solvent (100 mL or 100 g) is called its solubility at a given temperature. A solution that cannot dissolve any more solute at that temperature is a saturated solution. Temperature is mentioned because the solubility of a solid solute in a liquid solvent generally increases with temperature, whereas the solubility of gases dissolved in liquids generally decreases with an increase in temperature. Solubility is an important property used to separate substances from mixtures. A graph of solubility versus temperature is called a solubility curve, with temperature in degrees Celsius on the x-axis and solubility in grams per 100 g of water on the y-axis.

concepts.label: Crystallization
concepts.cardText: If a saturated solution of compound B made at 60 degrees Celsius is cooled gradually to 40 degrees, only the amount that matches its lower solubility remains in solution (241 g per 100 g of water) and the rest separates out as a pure solid, often as crystals. A crystal is a solid made up of particles arranged in a regular geometric pattern. Crystals form naturally, for example rock salt, candy sugar (mishri) and snowflakes formed when water vapour freezes in the air. In laboratories the process of forming crystals from a saturated solution is called crystallization. It can separate two solids when one is present in small quantity and both are soluble in the same solvent, and it can purify solids; its principle is the difference in the solubility of a substance at different temperatures. To make copper sulfate crystals the hot saturated solution is filtered to remove insoluble impurities and then cooled slowly without disturbing it, which gives the particles enough time to come together as larger, shiny, well-shaped crystals. Crystallization separates the desired pure substance from undesired impurities.

concepts.label: Distillation
concepts.cardText: A homogeneous mixture of two miscible liquids can be separated by heating the mixture until the liquid with the lower boiling point vaporises. The vapour is then cooled, turning back into liquid; this process is known as distillation. It allows the recovery of the solvent or the separation of liquids that differ in boiling point by at least about 25 degrees Celsius, and can also separate a liquid from a solution containing dissolved solids. The vapours of the lower-boiling liquid pass through a condenser where they are cooled, usually by circulating water or air, and condensed as a pure liquid collected in a separate vessel, while the solid or other liquid remains in the distillation flask. Acetone and water can be separated by distillation because acetone boils at about 56 degrees and water at 100 degrees, so one liquid vaporises before the vapours of the other form in significant amount. Distillation is used for extracting fragrances from flowers, as in Kannauj's Mitti ka Ittar by the Deg-Bhapka method. Fractional distillation separates components whose boiling points differ by less than 25 degrees, as in a petroleum refinery.

concepts.label: Paper Chromatography
concepts.cardText: When a drop of water falls on writing made with a black sketch pen, different colours may spread out. In Activity 5.5 a spot of black sketch pen ink is marked on a chromatography paper strip, the strip is placed vertically with its lower end dipping in water, and the water level must be below the spot. As the water rises the ink separates into different colour spots. This method is known as paper chromatography. It uses differences in the interactions of the components with the solvent and the paper to separate them; the liquid carries the substances up the paper, separating them based on how fast they move. Water may not work as a solvent in every case, and sometimes alcohol or a mixture of solvents is needed. The word chromatography comes from Greek words chroma, meaning colour, and graphein, meaning to write.

concepts.label: Separating Immiscible Liquids
concepts.cardText: Oil and water form separate layers; they do not mix and are called immiscible liquids. Sand and water do not mix, nor do iron filings and sulfur; these are heterogeneous mixtures. To separate mustard oil from water, the mixture is poured into a separating funnel and left undisturbed, when two layers form, with the yellow mustard oil as the upper layer and water as the lower layer. The stopcock is opened slowly to collect the lower layer of water carefully, closed when the water is almost fully drained, the small portion containing both liquids is discarded, and the oil is then collected separately. A separating funnel separates two immiscible liquids based on their different densities. Gas particles are free to move in all directions, so most mixtures of gases are homogeneous, while smoke, fog and dust in the air are heterogeneous mixtures with gas as one of the components.

concepts.label: Sublimation
concepts.cardText: In Activity 5.7 a mixture of crushed camphor and sand is heated gently in a china dish under an inverted funnel plugged with cotton. White solid camphor deposits on the inner wall of the funnel while the sand remains in the dish. Camphor, on heating below its melting point, changes directly from the solid state to the vapour state without passing through the liquid state; this process is called sublimation. On cooling, vapours condense back into a solid without becoming a liquid, which is called deposition. Camphor sublimes and separates from sand because sand does not sublime on heating. Naphthalene can be used in place of camphor, and solid carbon dioxide, known as dry ice, also undergoes sublimation.

concepts.label: Alloys: Solutions of Metals
concepts.cardText: Metals do not dissolve into each other at room temperature, but when metals are melted at high temperatures they can be mixed to form a solution. When such a hot mixture of two or more metals cools, it solidifies into a new material that appears to be a single metal. A homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or a metal and a non-metal, is called an alloy. Physical methods cannot separate the components of an alloy. Alloys are generally prepared to produce materials that are stronger, more rigid or more corrosion-resistant. Brass is approximately 80% copper and 20% zinc, bronze is approximately 80% copper and 20% tin, and stainless steel is usually iron with other elements such as carbon, chromium, nickel and molybdenum.

concepts.label: Suspensions
concepts.cardText: In a heterogeneous mixture in which solid particles, such as sand, do not dissolve but remain suspended throughout the bulk of the medium, such as water, the mixture is called a suspension. The particles of the undissolved substance are larger than the particles in a solution and are visible to the naked eye; sawdust in water and tea leaves in water are other examples. If muddy water is left undisturbed the heavier mud particles settle at the bottom, but the water may still appear cloudy. Filtering through cotton cloth or filter paper removes some larger particles but the water often remains cloudy, which shows that filtration is not always enough to separate tiny particles. In such cases techniques such as centrifugation and coagulation are used.

concepts.label: Centrifugation and the Paperfuge
concepts.cardText: Centrifugation involves spinning a mixture in a tube at a high speed. During centrifugation the tubes become horizontal and the centrifugal force, the outward force acting on a body moving in circular motion, causes the heavier particles to move outwards, where they settle at the bottom of the tube, while the lighter liquid remains at the top. It is widely used in laboratories to separate the components of blood, such as red blood cells and plasma, and in many chemical industries. A paperfuge is a simple hand-powered device, based on a common toy, that can perform the same process without electricity; by spinning blood samples at a very high speed it separates heavier components from lighter ones, and this low-cost tool can help detect diseases like malaria and anaemia in remote areas.

concepts.label: Coagulation
concepts.cardText: Powdered alum (fitkari), a white crystalline chemical substance often used in water purification, can be added to muddy water. The alum causes the fine suspended particles to clump together. This process is called coagulation and the alum is said to act as a coagulant. The larger clumps settle by gravity (sedimentation) and can be separated from the water by decantation or filtration. The formation of cheese (paneer) from milk also involves coagulation, in which an acid such as lemon juice or vinegar is used as a coagulant, causing the coagulation of milk proteins.

concepts.label: Colloids
concepts.cardText: Blood can be separated by centrifugation and coagulates, yet its cells cannot be seen with the naked eye. Blood is neither a solution nor a true suspension; it is a colloid. Other examples of colloids are milk, tomato sauce and ice cream. Solutions, suspensions and colloids differ mainly in the size of the dissolved or suspended particles: the particle size is the smallest, less than 1 nm in diameter, in a solution; colloids have larger particles, 1 to 1000 nm; and suspensions have much larger particles, more than 1000 nm in diameter. Unlike a suspension, the particles in a colloid do not settle over time from the mixture and are uniformly dispersed throughout as in a solution. The components of a colloid are called the dispersed phase, the solute-like component or dispersed particles, and the dispersion medium, the component in which the dispersed phase is suspended.

concepts.label: The Tyndall Effect
concepts.cardText: When a laser beam is passed through three beakers, the path of the light beam is not visible in solution A, while the particles in suspension B scatter, or spread, the beam making its path visible. In mixture C too the path of light is visible, indicating that the particles scattered the light though the mixture appeared homogeneous. The scattering of light by particles is known as the Tyndall effect, called so because it was first explained by John Tyndall. It can also be seen when a fine beam of light enters a dark room through a small hole, because light gets scattered by the dust and smoke particles in the air, or in the floodlights of a stadium. Scattering of light occurs when it passes through a colloid or a suspension but not when it passes through a transparent solution.

concepts.label: Emulsions
concepts.cardText: Some common colloids have both the dispersed phase and the dispersion medium as liquids; these are called emulsions. Emulsions containing oil and water are classified as oil-in-water or water-in-oil, depending on the nature of the dispersed phase and the dispersion medium. Milk and vanishing creams are common examples of oil-in-water emulsions, whereas butter, body lotions and cold cream are examples of water-in-oil emulsions. Some medicines are prepared as emulsions to disperse them in water and make them easily palatable, which also reduces the greasy feeling of the liquid medicine. The presence of emulsifying agents stabilises emulsions; for example proteins in milk and butter act as emulsifying agents.

concepts.label: Separation of Mixtures in Daily Life and Nature
concepts.cardText: We use various properties, such as size, density and solubility, to separate mixtures, but separation is not always simple; it is hard to separate all the ingredients of a lemonade. Separation happens in nature and in our bodies too: our kidneys remove waste from our blood. Cleaning oceans and rivers by removing plastic waste and treating sewage before releasing it into the environment are bigger challenges. Sewage treatment involves steps such as sedimentation, coagulation and filtration, and the clean water can be reused for flushing toilets or watering plants. Dry waste such as plastic, paper, glass and metal can be recycled while wet waste like food scraps and vegetable peels can be composted, and researchers are finding ways to recover valuable materials such as lithium from old batteries.
